missing_spec_content.spec_text: The weight of an object may be considered to act at a single point referred to as the object’s ‘centre of mass’.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson never mentions centre of mass.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: The weight of an object and the mass of an object are directly proportional.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson gives W = mg but never says that weight is directly proportional to mass.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should recognise and be able to use the symbol for proportionality, ∝
missing_spec_content.why: The ∝ symbol does not appear and is not taught.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Weight is measured using a calibrated spring-balance (a newtonmeter).
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson does not say how weight is measured. Spring-balance and newtonmeter are never mentioned.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: The weight of an object may be considered to act at a single point referred to as the object’s ‘centre of mass’.
missing_spec_content.why: Neither the idea nor the term is covered in any key point, table or revision bullet.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to describe the similarities and distinctions between the planets, their moons, and artificial satellites.
missing_spec_content.why: There is no comparison of planets, moons and artificial satellites. The intro only says gravity 'keeps planets in orbit around stars and moons in orbit around planets'.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: (HT only) for circular orbits, the force of gravity can lead to changing velocity but unchanged speed
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson never explains that in a circular orbit the velocity changes (its direction changes) while the speed stays constant.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: (HT only) for a stable orbit, the radius must change if the speed changes.
missing_spec_content.why: This is only partly covered. The lesson links higher orbits to lower speed, but never states that a change in speed requires a change in radius for a stable orbit. Instead it says a wrong speed means escaping or falling back (see factual_errors).

above_gcse.text: The gravitational field is shown by field lines pointing towards the centre of the mass. They show the direction of the force on a small test mass.
above_gcse.why: Gravitational field lines and 'test mass' are not in the specification sections given. This is A-level style field treatment.

above_gcse.text: Gravity provides the centripetal force that keeps the object in its curved path.
above_gcse.why: The specification says only that 'Gravity provides the force that allows planets and satellites ... to maintain their circular orbits'. The term 'centripetal force' is not used in these sections.

above_gcse.text: Don't just say 'gravity keeps it going round'. Say 'gravity provides the centripetal force needed for circular motion'.
above_gcse.why: This tells students they must use a term the specification sections do not require. It may make students think the spec wording is not enough.

above_gcse.text: But it also has a high tangential velocity (sideways speed).
above_gcse.why: 'Tangential velocity' is not specification terminology at this level.

above_gcse.text: The result is a circular (or elliptical) orbit.
above_gcse.why: The specification deals only with circular orbits. Elliptical orbits are not required and are not explained.

above_gcse.text: Geostationary satellites: 24-hour period, same position above Earth
above_gcse.why: Geostationary satellites are not in the specification sections given. They are also not taught anywhere in the lesson body but appear on the revision card.

factual_errors.text: Near Earth's surface, the field is roughly uniform (the same in all directions near the surface).
factual_errors.correction: A uniform field has the same strength and the same direction at every point. 'The same in all directions' is not what uniform means.

factual_errors.text: For a circular orbit at a fixed height, the speed must be exactly right. Too fast, and the object escapes. Too slow, and it falls back to Earth.
factual_errors.correction: A small change in speed does not make the object escape or crash. It moves to a different orbit: for a stable orbit, the radius must change if the speed changes. Escape needs a much larger speed (escape velocity). A small decrease gives a lower or elliptical orbit, not necessarily a fall to Earth.

factual_errors.text: Higher orbits: the gravitational field is weaker, so less centripetal force is needed. The orbital speed is lower.
factual_errors.correction: The causation is reversed. The gravitational force on the satellite is weaker at a greater radius, so less centripetal force is provided. A smaller speed is therefore needed for a stable orbit at that radius. The force needed is set by speed and radius, not by the field.

factual_errors.text: Not using g = 9.8 N/kg in calculations. The gravitational field strength on Earth is 9.8 N/kg. Use 10 N/kg only if told to round. Always check which value the exam question specifies.
factual_errors.correction: The specification states: '(In any calculation the value of the gravitational field strength (g) will be given.)' Students should use the value given in the question. They are not expected to supply 9.8 N/kg themselves or decide when to round.

wrong_terms.text: Gravity provides the centripetal force that keeps the object in its curved path.
wrong_terms.spec_term: Gravity provides the force that allows planets and satellites (both natural and artificial) to maintain their circular orbits

checkpoint_mismatch.checkpoint: checkpoints[1]: "Why does a satellite in a higher orbit travel more slowly than one in a lower orbit?"
checkpoint_mismatch.why: The checkpoint tests orbital speed against height. That idea is taught only in keyPoints[2]. KeyPoints[1] covers field definition, field lines and decrease with distance, and says nothing about orbital speed. The marked answer also repeats the reversed reasoning 'less centripetal force, and therefore less speed, is needed' (see factual_errors).

not_checked: examTips[3]: "Examiners use it in every set of papers." This claim about exam frequency cannot be checked against the specification text.
